abstract: Objective: This study aimed to evaluate network brain activity across both cortical and deep brain (ventral-capsule/ventral-striatum; VC/VS) sites in patients with Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) that were receiving DBS treatment. We sought to identify relationships between activity in both brain sites, and interactions between them, with evolution of OCD symptomology over treatment. We hypothesized that recordings from cortical sites would carry unique informational content that could predict symptoms and support future adaptive stimulation designs. Materials and Methods: Two patients with severe treatment refractory OCD were implanted with electrodes targeting VC/VS and the supplementary motor area (SMA) bilaterally. Electrodes were connected to Medtronic implantable pulse generators (PC+S or Percept) and could both deliver stimulation and record ongoing local field potential activity. Patients underwent approximately two years of stimulation treatment during which clinical measures of OCD symptoms and brain recordings were regularly collected. Results: Spectral features of VCVS and SMA brain activity had significantly higher entropy (information content) in the signal recorded from the cortical site. A mass univariate partial correlation analysis, controlling for confounders, revealed that cortical and VCVS-cortical interactions were highly represented among the features significantly associated with symptom evolution over the course of treatment (Patient 1: 20 of 30 significant features; Patient 2: 22 of 30 significant features; permutation based false discovery rate correction at q < 0.05). Conclusions: Our findings underscore the importance of capturing cortical activity and VCVS-cortical interactions during DBS research for OCD, with potential implications for the development of more informed and personalized stimulation strategies, including adaptive DBS.
